title: Eggheads at Anthropic Said They Used Claude to "Solve" Humor
source_used: Futurism (pre-fetched full text), which relays a New York Magazine interview
key_facts: Futurism reports that Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee best known for quitting and claiming the AI industry was 'gambling with our lives', gave a new interview to New York Magazine.
Coxon recalls that when he joined there was a Slack channel with a Claude chatbot 'trained to solve humor' and colleagues saying 'we solved humor'.
He says he replied in the chat that they had clearly not solved humor.
Coxon described 'groupthink dynamics' at Anthropic that sometimes made him feel like the odd man out, and acknowledged Anthropic could be described as a cult, though he called that an 'extreme' view.
Futurism treats the anecdote as a sign that AI builders can be out of touch and notes Anthropic openly raises the possibility that AI models could be conscious.
The article gives no reply from Anthropic and does not date the anecdote beyond 'when I first joined'.
quote_evidence: When I first joined, there was a Slack channel with a Claude that had been trained to solve humor,
And I was in the chat like, 'No, you haven't. You clearly haven't solved humor. What the hell is this?'
In a new interview with New York Magazine, Coxon recalled some of the "groupthink dynamics" he saw taking hold at Anthropic
why_it_matters_hint: It is a light insider story about how one AI company's staff treated a chatbot, told by one critic.
event_date: New York Magazine interview described as new on 10 Oct 2026; the Slack-channel anecdote itself is undated (when Coxon first joined Anthropic).
notes: Futurism relays a New York Magazine interview, so New York Magazine is the first reporter; its own page was not found or read, and the entry links the Futurism page where the text was read. The anecdote is one former employee's memory; Futurism's wording is mocking and the headline presents it as Anthropic's claim.
